name: Anatomy
tagline: A Claude skill that turns a one-line description into an interactive, labeled diagram you can take apart in your browser.
sentence: Ask Claude to explain how something works and it builds an interactive picture of the real machine - hover to see parts move, click to take it apart, read the live numbers.

visual.alt: An isometric illustration of a SpaceX Raptor 2 rocket engine on a test stand, firing with red-orange exhaust. Labels read 'Fig 1', 'RAPTOR 2 - TEST STAND', 'Pc 300 bar - 230 tf'. A 'SHUT DOWN' button and 'HOVER THE ENGINE TO TAKE IT APART' instruction appear at bottom.
visual.caption: An anatomy illustration of a Raptor 2 engine - the kind of interactive, labeled diagram the skill creates from a plain-English request.

board.say: You want to explain how a machine or system works, but drawing a clear, labeled diagram by hand takes hours - and a screenshot or stock image does not show the insides.
board.eg: You are writing docs for a caching system and want a picture that shows how the parts fit together, not just a box-and-arrow chart.

board.say: You type a one-line request in Claude Code (or another supported coding agent) and the skill takes over.
board.eg: Type '/anatomy explain how a pin-tumbler lock works, interactive' and the agent starts building.

board.say: A plain-English description of the machine or idea you want illustrated.
board.eg: 'Explain how a Raptor 2 rocket engine works' - one sentence is enough.

board.say: Claude writes a computational model with real values, then draws each part as a shaded solid and wires them together into a moving figure.
steps: Writes the working values (pressures, temperatures, speeds) as a model that drives the motion and the readout
Draws 40 to 150+ parts with four-tone shading, assembles them in the right order, and adds labels
Runs a geometry audit to check that no parts overlap or pass through each other, then takes screenshots to verify the result
board.eg: The Raptor 2 example: 11 assemblies, a WebGL exhaust plume, and a live readout showing chamber pressure and thrust.

board.say: An interactive diagram you can open in a browser, embed in docs, or drop into a React app.

outputs.eg: A single file you open in any browser - hover the engine to take it apart, see each part labeled
Drop a component into your Next.js docs site with working interaction and keyboard support
Fire, water, exhaust, lamp glow and steam layered into the diagram for realism

before: Explaining how a machine works means drawing a diagram by hand, paying a technical illustrator, or settling for a flat screenshot that does not show the insides.
A box-and-arrow chart gets the topology across but does not show what the parts look like or how they move.
after: Describe what you want in one sentence and get an interactive picture where every part is labeled, moves realistically, and shows live numbers.
The diagram is source code you own - a standalone HTML file, an SVG, or a React component you drop into your docs.

steps: Install the skill: run `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g` (requires [Node.js 20.10+](https://nodejs.org/)). If you use Claude Code, add `-a claude-code`.
In Claude Code, type `/anatomy explain how a dial indicator works, interactive`. The agent will build a figure - a small one takes 30-90 minutes of agent time.
View the result in your browser. Hover the parts to see them labeled, click to take them apart, and check the live readout.
try.paste:
/skillspector https://github.com/wheresryan22/anatomy

If that scan passes: install with `npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a claude-code`, then run `/anatomy explain how a dial indicator works, interactive`. The small example takes about 30-90 minutes of agent time.

footprint.disk: About 10 MB for the skill folder (including examples). No additional packages to install - uses only Node.js built-in modules.
footprint.memory: No data found. Chrome or Chromium is needed only for the visual verification step. WebGL is needed for shader effects but the plain SVG renders without it.
footprint.runs_on: Any system that runs a supported coding agent (Claude Code, Antigravity, OpenCode, Codex, MiniMax Code) and Node.js 20.10+. Output works in any modern browser. Reduced-motion mode stops all animation.

best_for: You want to explain a machine or system visually and do not want to draw it yourself - one sentence in, interactive diagram out
You are writing technical docs or a presentation and want a labeled, interactive figure you can embed as HTML, SVG or a React component
skip_if: You need a chart with axes and data plots - this draws machines and instruments, not bar charts or line graphs
You need a quick illustration in minutes - a single figure takes 30 minutes to 2+ hours of agent time, and complex ones (a turbofan engine) took 14 hours in one test

alternatives.name: Mermaid
alternatives.line: Text-to-diagram tool for flowcharts, sequence diagrams and architecture charts. Fast and widely supported, but draws flat boxes and arrows, not shaded machines.

alternatives.name: Excalidraw
alternatives.line: A free whiteboard for hand-drawn-style diagrams. Good for quick sketches, but you draw by hand - no AI generation.

alternatives.name: draw.io (diagrams.net)
alternatives.line: A free diagram editor with shape libraries. More control over layout, but no isometric shading or interactive disassembly.

watch: **Figures take a long time to build.** A small dial gauge takes 30-90 minutes of active agent time. A Raptor 2 engine took over 10 hours. A turbofan took 14 hours. Each hour uses Claude Code usage quota.

**This is not an engineering simulation.** The diagrams look detailed, but one reviewer notes they do not establish engineering accuracy, manufacturing suitability, or a validated simulation. The numbers shown are illustrative, not certified.
**8 days old - no production use yet.** The repo was created October 8, 2026. No named users or teams have reported using it in production. Stars show interest, not adoption.
**Review the skill before installing.** It runs Node scripts and a headless Chrome browser locally. The publish script reads duration and token usage from session logs unless you pass `--no-session`.
